title: Climate Set by Earth's Orbit
question: How can slow changes in the way Earth moves alter its climate?
hook: Earth is closest to the Sun in January, right in the middle of northern winter.
idea: Slow changes in Earth's orbit shape, axial tilt and axis direction shift where and when sunlight arrives, shaping climate over thousands of years.

beats.prompt: Over thousands of years, the tilt of Earth's axis grows a little larger. What happens to the seasons?

choices.label: They become milder
choices.feedback: It seems a tilt change might even things out, but more tilt does the opposite.

choices.label: Nothing changes, since tilt only affects day length
choices.feedback: Tilt does more than set day length; it changes how sharply the seasons differ.

beats.explain: A greater tilt makes the seasons more extreme.

beats.prompt: Match each term to what it describes.
pairs: How far the orbit departs from a circle
Change in the direction the axis points
Main pull changing the orbit's shape
beats.explain: Each of the three movements changes a different part of Earth's motion, and the giant planets' gravity mainly drives the change in orbit shape.

beats.prompt: Sort each feature of Earth's motion by whether it varies over time or stays constant.
beats.explain: The orbit's shape, the tilt and the axis direction all change, but the semi-major axis is invariant, and so is the year it sets.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning about northern seasons is wrong; which?
steps: Earth moves fastest when it is nearest the Sun.
Earth is now nearest the Sun around 3 January.
So Earth passes through northern winter quickly.
So northern winter lasts longer than northern summer.
beats.explain: Moving quickly through winter makes it shorter: northern summer is 4.66 days longer than winter.
